segments.english: Great is the Torah, in that it gives life to those who practice it in this world and in the world to come, as it is said: For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all his flesh. And it says: It shall be healing to your navel and refreshment to your bones. And it says: It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it, and those who support it are happy. And it says: For they are a wreath of grace for your head and necklaces for your throat. And it says: She will give to your head a wreath of grace; a crown of splendor she will present to you. And it says: For through me your days will increase, and years of life will be added to you. And it says: Length of days is in her right hand; in her left hand, wealth and honor. And it says: For length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you. And it says: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.

grammar: גְּדוֹלָה תוֹרָה: the predicate adjective comes first, so the sentence reads "great is the Torah".
שֶׁהִיא נוֹתֶנֶת: a participle in a שֶׁ-clause that gives the reason; לְעֹשֶׂיהָ is a participle with a feminine suffix, "to its doers".
The chain of proof texts is joined by וְאוֹמֵר, "and it says", each introducing one more verse; שם "ibid." gives the book and the next token gives the chapter.
In the quoted verses the feminine Torah (Wisdom in Proverbs) is the subject of תִּתֵּן, תְּמַגְּנֶךָּ and the suffixes -הּ, -הָ.
וְיוֹסִיפוּ and יוֹסִיפוּ are third-person plural with no stated subject, so the English uses the passive.
segments.note: The citations of chapter and book are left out of the reading text and given in the apparatus. Rendered literally, תִּפְאֶרֶת is "splendor" throughout the unit, and שָׁרֶךָ is "your navel" (the sense in Prov 3:8).
apparatus: Vilna spells several words without vowel letters or differently (לעושיה, למוצאיהם, ותומכיה, מאושר, לגרגרותיך, תמגניך, אורך, עושר) and omits some of the citation tokens (שם ג etc.).

segments.english: Rabbi Shimon son of Yehudah, in the name of Rabbi Shimon son of Yochai, says: Beauty, strength, wealth, honor, wisdom, old age, gray hair, and children are fitting for the righteous and fitting for the world, as it is said: Gray hair is a crown of splendor; in the way of righteousness it is found. And it says: The splendor of young men is their strength, and the glory of the old is gray hair. And it says: The crown of the wise is their wealth. And it says: The crown of the old is children's children, and the splendor of children is their fathers. And it says: The moon will be abashed and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders is glory. Rabbi Shimon son of Menasya says: These seven qualities that the sages enumerated for the righteous, all of them were fulfilled in Rabbi and in his sons.

grammar: מִשּׁוּם introduces the tradition: "in the name of", literally "on account of".
The eight terms of the list each take the article; נָאֶה is a singular adjective predicated of the whole list, "fitting".
שֶׁמָּנוּ is a relative clause, "that they counted"; נִתְקַיְּמוּ is Nitpael, a late stem with reflexive-passive sense, "were fulfilled".
The verses use poetic parallelism (crown // splendor); Isaiah 24:23 has חָפְרָה, from חפר "to be ashamed", and בוש.
segments.note: The Hebrew list has eight terms (beauty, strength, wealth, honor, wisdom, old age, gray hair, children) while R. Shimon son of Menasya speaks of seven qualities; the difficulty is kept and not smoothed over. רַבִּי in the last clause is Rabbi Yehudah the Patriarch. The pack gives חָפַר "to dig" as the lemma of וְחָפְרָה; the English follows the verse, חפר "to be abashed" (a homograph).

segments.english: Rabbi Yose son of Kisma said: Once I was walking on the road and a certain man met me, and he greeted me, and I returned his greeting. He said to me: Rabbi, from what place are you? I said to him: I am from a great city of sages and of scribes. He said to me: Rabbi, is it your wish to dwell with us in our place? And I will give you a thousand thousand dinars of gold and precious stones and pearls. I said to him: My son, if you give me all the silver and gold and precious stones and pearls that are in the world, I dwell nowhere except in a place of Torah. And not only that, but at the hour of a person's departure nothing accompanies a person: neither silver nor gold nor precious stones or pearls, but only Torah and good deeds. as it is said: When you walk, it will lead you; when you lie down, it will watch over you; and when you awake, it will talk with you. When you walk, it will lead you in this world; when you lie down, it will watch over you in the grave; and when you awake, it will talk with you in the world to come. And so it is written in the Book of Psalms by the hand of David, king of Israel: The Torah of Your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver. And it says: Mine is the silver and mine is the gold, says the LORD of hosts.

grammar: The story is told in the first person with a perfect plus participle (הָיִיתִי מְהַלֵּךְ), "I was walking".
נָתַן שָׁלוֹם is an idiom for giving a greeting; הֶחֱזִיר שָׁלוֹם, "returned a greeting".
אֵינִי דָר אֶלָּא "I dwell only/nowhere but" is a negative with אֶלָּא: exclusive sense.
אֵין מְלַוִּין is a plural participle with no stated subject (impersonal), followed by a list governed by לֹא ... וְלֹא.
The verse is quoted twice: first whole, then split into its three clauses, each tied to a world (this world, the grave, the world to come).
מֵאַלְפֵי זָהָב וָכָסֶף: "than thousands of gold and silver", with an understood unit of coin.
segments.note: מֵעִיר גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁל חֲכָמִים: the particle שֶׁל is mishnaic; the dinars of gold are dinars (דִּינָר). The sentence about what accompanies a person is impersonal in Hebrew ("they do not accompany him"); the English gives the sense of the plural participle without a subject.
apparatus: Vilna omits some citation tokens (משלי ו, תהלים קיט, חגי ב).

segments.english: Five possessions the Holy One, blessed be He, acquired for Himself in His world, and these are they: Torah, one possession; heaven and earth, one possession; Abraham, one possession; Israel, one possession; the Temple, one possession. Torah: from where do we know it? For it is written The LORD acquired me as the beginning of His way, before His works of old. Heaven and earth, one possession: from where do we know it? For it is written Thus says the LORD: The heavens are my throne and the earth is My footstool; what house is it that you would build for Me and what is the place of My rest? And it says: How many are Your works, O LORD; You made them all in wisdom; the earth is full of Your possessions. Abraham, one possession: from where do we know it? For it is written And he blessed him and said: Blessed be Abram to God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth. Israel, one possession: from where do we know it? For it is written Until Your people pass over, O LORD, until the people You acquired pass over. And it says: As for the holy ones who are in the land, they, and the majestic ones, all my delight is in them. The Temple, one possession: from where do we know it? For it is written The place for Your dwelling You made, O LORD; the sanctuary, O LORD, Your hands established. And it says: And He brought them to the border of His holiness, this mountain that His right hand acquired.

grammar: קִנְיָן is a noun of the form קִנְיָן "acquisition, possession", from קנה; the mishnah reads the verb קנה in each verse as "acquire".
מִנַּיִן is the formula that asks for the proof text: "from where [do we learn it]?"; דִּכְתִיב "for it is written" introduces the answer.
וְאֵלּוּ הֵן, "and these are they", introduces the list.
Heaven and earth form one possession: שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ is the paired phrase, with both nouns under one קִנְיָן אֶחָד.
In the verses, qal participle קֹנֵה (construct) governs שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ; Exodus 15:16 repeats עַד יַעֲבֹר and זוּ is a relative pronoun.
segments.note: In Prov 8:22 קָנָנִי may also mean "created me"; the mishnah reads "acquired", and the English follows it. For Gen 14:19 קֹנֵה may be "maker" or "possessor"; "possessor" matches the point of the mishnah. The pack marks לְאֵל (Gen 14:19) and אֶל (Ps 78:54) with the lemma אַל; the data is kept, and the words are the noun "God" and the preposition "to".
apparatus: Vilna adds קנין אחד at one point where the base has none.

segments.english: Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He did not create it except for His glory, as it is said: Everyone who is called by My name and for My glory I created him, I formed him, indeed I made him. And it says: The LORD will reign forever and ever. Rabbi Hananya son of Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments, as it is said: The LORD was pleased for the sake of His righteousness to magnify Torah and make it glorious.

grammar: כָּל מַה שֶּׁ- "everything that": כָּל plus the indefinite relative מַה, then the relative שֶׁ.
לֹא ... אֶלָּא "not ... except": "He created it only for His glory".
In Isaiah 43:7 three verbs in the perfect (בְּרָאתִיו, יְצַרְתִּיו, עֲשִׂיתִיו) with a pronoun suffix form a rising series: created, formed, made.
לְזַכּוֹת is the infinitive of זכה in the Hifil sense "to give merit to, to make worthy".
In Isaiah 42:21 the imperfect יַגְדִּיל ... וְיַאְדִּיר is read as the purpose of חָפֵץ: "to magnify ... and make glorious".
segments.note: In Exodus 15:18 the divine name is written with vowels in the pack; English renders "the LORD". In Isaiah 42:21, לְמַעַן צִדְקוֹ is "for the sake of His righteousness" and the verse is quoted in the form of the mishnah.
apparatus: Vilna reads אמר where the base has no word at one point.
